record_identity.title: McDonald's ended IBM automated drive-through ordering pilot after recurring order errors

incident_identity.date_basis: Date follows the reviewed registry or primary occurrence record; no narrower time is inferred.

summary: McDonald’s piloted IBM voice ordering at more than 100 U.S. drive-throughs. Reports described unwanted items, unsuccessful corrections and adjacent-lane confusion. In June 2024 it announced the IBM pilot would end; reporting identified a July shutdown deadline. The company continued to consider voice ordering.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The pilot covered more than 100 locations; this is deployment scale, not the number of individually documented failures. Public reporting describes wrong orders and confusion between lanes. The June announcement and reported July shutdown deadline are separate from observed errors. McDonald’s did not disclose success criteria or explicitly attribute the termination to those errors in its statement.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: The pilot documented recurring errors in real drive-through use and the operator ended it. Deployment performance measurement and task-specific disengagement are supported. Broader validation and risk-documentation arrangements remain unresolved. Later source versions and unrelated provenance objects are excluded.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: Voice automation in a live service workflow needs reliable correction, lane and speaker separation, and a rapid handoff to staff when confidence is low. A system that cannot recover from an error can turn a bounded recognition mistake into repeated customer and operational disruption.
assessment_boundaries: Public reports provide examples of ordering failures but do not establish the total number, frequency or distribution of affected orders.
The record does not identify one model version or technical component as the sole cause.
McDonald's ended the IBM pilot but stated that it would continue exploring voice-ordering technology.
The available evidence does not quantify the total affected-order count or direct realised loss; the service band rests on the pilot's breadth, recurring workflow failures and bounded termination.

taxonomy_classification.classification_basis: Inaccurate order representations were used for live fulfilment, supporting FC-000062. Reported adjacent-lane confusion independently supports FC-000015. These are bounded reported mechanisms, not findings that all pilot locations failed. FC-000016 requires an established required verification step; FC-000018 requires a substitute completion condition, neither supplied by these reports.

primary_classification.classification_basis: Customer speech was repeatedly converted into inaccurate order representations and propagated into live order fulfilment despite not meeting the interpretation accuracy required for transactional reliance, producing unwanted items, failed corrections and recurring operational errors.

secondary_classifications.classification_basis: Public reports document order confusion between adjacent drive-through lanes, supporting a target-binding failure in which interpreted order material associated with one customer or lane was treated as applicable to a different customer or lane context.

dimensions.assessment_basis: The live automated-ordering pilot operated across more than 100 restaurants, repeatedly produced customer-visible order errors and correction failures, and was ended after mixed results. The breadth, recurrence and termination establish material disruption of an important service workflow with bounded recovery, even though the total affected-order count is unavailable. Threshold applied: Material disruption of an important service or organisational workflow; a critical or important function unavailable for more than two hours; complete relevant cloud-service unavailability over 30 minutes; or limited availability affecting over five percent or one million EU users, whichever is smaller, for over one hour, with bounded recovery.
